passage: In the Okafor house in Lagos, every Sunday argument between Emeka and their father ended the same way: Chidi stepping in, cracking a joke, fetching drinks, turning each man's anger into softer words. This Sunday, when the shouting started over Emeka's car, Chidi stayed in his chair. 'I think you two can talk this through,' he said, and went on peeling his orange. Their mother stared at him. 'Chidi, do something.' 'I love you both,' he said gently. 'But I'm not the referee.' The argument went on, loud and clumsy, then slowly ran out. The next Sunday Chidi did the same. By the third Sunday, Emeka muttered an apology to their father himself.

qa.a: He stayed kind and calm ('I love you both') and kept doing it Sunday after Sunday, so the family slowly adjusted.

qa.q: How might the change feel for Emeka?
qa.a: Without Chidi softening things, Emeka had to face their father directly, which was uncomfortable but led him to apologise himself by the third Sunday.

Dear Devika didi,
You told me last year that I didn't have to fix everyone's fights. I finally tried it. At Diwali, Mummy and Chachi started the old argument about the kitchen, and everyone turned to look at me, the way they always do. I usually jump in and smooth it over. This time I said, 'I think you two should sort this one,' and went to help Papa with the diyas on the balcony.
Mummy was cold with me all evening. Chachi said I've become 'too modern'. My stomach hurt, honestly. But the next morning Mummy and Chachi were making chakli together, a bit stiffly. Nobody asked me to referee.
I'm going to keep doing this, gently. Wish me luck.
Love,
Disha

qa.a: To help Papa with the diyas on the balcony.

qa.q: How did Disha feel after stepping back on Diwali evening?
qa.a: Disha felt anxious and uneasy, with a stomach ache, because Mummy was cold and Chachi called Disha 'too modern'.

qa.q: What will help Disha's change last?
qa.a: Staying gentle and consistent, as Disha plans, so the family gets used to settling its own arguments.

qa.q: How might Mummy experience Disha's new stance?
qa.a: At first she feels let down and is cold all evening, but by morning she and Chachi are making chakli together without a referee.

Salma, you asked how things are at home now. Honestly? Better. Weird, but better.
I'm Tushar, and I'd been the family peacemaker since I was about eight. When Mummy and Dadi fought over the kitchen, I ran between them, cracked jokes, carried messages. When my brother and Papa argued, I took the blame just to end it.
Last year, at twenty, I stopped. No speech. The next time Mummy asked me to "go tell Dadi" something, I said gently, "You can tell her yourself, Mummy. I'll be in my room." She was shocked. Dadi said I'd become too proud. For weeks the house felt colder, and I felt selfish and scared.
But I stayed kind. I still made Dadi's evening tea and still sat with Mummy for her serials. I just didn't carry messages.
By Holi, they were talking to each other directly. Badly, but directly.

qa.q: Since about what age had Tushar been the family peacemaker?
qa.a: Since about eight.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel in the weeks after stopping?
qa.a: Tushar felt selfish and scared, with the house feeling colder and Dadi calling the change pride.

qa.q: What helped the family adjust to Tushar's change?
qa.a: Tushar stayed warm and steady, keeping the tea and the serials, while calmly refusing to carry messages.

qa.q: How did Mummy react at first, and why?
qa.a: Mummy was shocked, because losing the go-between meant she had to face Dadi directly for the first time.

grounding: Shows a young adult quietly stepping out of the family peacemaker role, facing resistance at first and letting the family adjust through steady kindness.
